subject: Bespoke bars and entertaining furniture
hook: Not every edge on a cabinet needs the same edging. On a bar, the front edge earns the thickest.
ig:
Not every edge on a cabinet needs the same edging. On a bar, the front edge earns the thickest.

ABS edge banding comes in different thicknesses, and choosing the right one for each edge is one of those details nobody notices until it is wrong.

How we think about it:
• 2 mm on the edges that face the room and take the knocks: bar fronts, worktop edges, door edges near seating
• 1 mm on visible edges that see less contact, such as shelf fronts
• 0.4 mm on internal and hidden edges, where it seals the board but never gets bumped

Thicker edging gives the edge more to absorb a knock before the board beneath is exposed. On a bar, where stools get pulled in and bottles get set down at speed, that matters.

It is the same reasoning we apply to kitchens and hallway storage. Save this for when you are asking your maker questions.
fb:
Here is a detail you will probably never notice, unless someone gets it wrong: the thickness of the edging on your furniture.

On a home bar, the front edges get a hard life. Stools bump into them, bags swing past, bottles get put down quickly. So we use thicker ABS edging on those room-facing edges, and thinner edging on shelves and hidden edges where it is just there to seal the board.

Protection goes where the wear is. If you are planning furniture for entertaining, this is a good question to ask whoever builds it. See what we make here:
